title: Trump’s diesel deal with Putin angers Ukraine as experts doubt impact on prices | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has slammed an agreement on diesel fuel between the US and Russia, casting the decision as an “investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged.”

US President Donald Trump on Friday said he secured a deal from Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to supply markets with Russian diesel fuel as he works to bring down energy costs ahead of the midterm elections.

Zelensky said the move, which Trump announced as fresh Ukraine-US talks were getting underway in Miami, was “a weak decision of strong partners,” while analysts said the agreement was not likely to lower diesel prices in any meaningful way.

“We need strong signals from the United States, from Europe, and from other partners — signals in support of Ukraine and aimed at LIMITING Russia’s ability to wage war and terrorize people,” Zelensky said. Hours after Trump’s announcement Russian strikes killed at least 17 people in Ukraine.

Trump wrote onsocial mediathat Putin agreed to “immediately supply” more than 300,000 tons of diesel to global energy markets, with another 500,000 tons promised in November. Together, the amounts — equal to 6 million barrels of diesel fuel — would cover about a day and a half worth of US demand, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

But former US officials said it is unclear if Putin even has the amount of diesel that Trump cited to sell, as Ukrainian strikes put growing strain on the country’s oil supplies.

Just this week, Kyiv has claimed strikes on five different refineries across Russia, the latest of which were announced by Ukrainian authorities after Trump’s Friday announcement.

Trump said that millions more tons of Russian diesel would be supplied following the first tranches “based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries.”

Analysts cast doubt on the impact of the agreement.

“We are talking PERHAPS a 5-6% increase in supply between now and year end,” Dan Pickering, founder and chief investment officer at Pickering Energy Partners, said about the the president’s announcement.

“Bottom line — this is helpful but not a needle mover for global diesel markets,” Pickering said. “Sidenote — there is a reason Trump talked about volumes in tons instead of barrels. The tons number looks bigger to a general observer. This is more politics than a game changer.”

Russiabanned exports of dieselin early July, after Ukrainian drone strikes on its refineries triggered widespread fuel shortages across the country. This cut roughly 800,000 barrels per day from the global market — at a time when supplies were already tight because of the US war against Iran.

According to the Kremlin readout of the phone call between the two leaders, Putin told Trump that Russia was “ready to supply oil and petroleum products to the US and global markets.”

“I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy,” Putin said, according to the Kremlin.

But analysts — and commodities traders — raised doubts that Russia would be able to live up to that promise.

At the close of trading on Friday, diesel futures were down by about 4%.

Kyiv has long advocated for tougher sanctions on Russian energy exports, arguing that oil and gas revenues are a major source of funding for Russia’s war machine.

The US president has blamed the rise in global diesel prices on the Ukraine-Russia war andcalled on both sidesto halt strikes on energy facilities as recently as last month, to little avail.

The past few months have been brutal for Ukrainian civilians as Russia has taken advantage of Kyiv’s critical shortage of air defense missiles, launching near non-stop aerial attacks against Ukrainian cities. One such strike on a bus stop in eastern Ukrainekilled more than 30people on Thursday.

More recently, a Russian attack on Ukraine’s southeastern Zaporizhzhia region killed 17 people, including three children, local authorities said Saturday. Search and rescue operations are ongoing.

Zelensky has made it clear the timing of the announcement — just as a top-level Ukrainian delegation arrived to Miami for talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner — makes it all the more painful for Kyiv.

“In this exact moment when our team is talking to the American team in Florida, the US President has a conversation with Kremlin leader, with the leader of this war, the leader of this aggression,” he said.

Richard Nephew, a former principal deputy coordinator for sanctions policy at the State Department, noted that “the message it sends and the damage it does to the broader sanctions regime is very significant.”

“How does anyone take the sanctions regime seriously?” he questioned, noting that if the US is going to say that they need to use sanctions relief to address an economic issue, “how can we convincingly argue that anyone else shouldn’t use the same excuse?”

A former senior State Department official said it doesn’t matter if Putin can actually deliver the diesel because “now he’s achieved the result he wants” which is Trump thinking he’s gotten a pre-election bump and it might have an impact on the markets.

The timing of the call with the start of the talks with Ukraine is no coincidence.

“Putin is a lot of things, but he’s not stupid,” they said.

Trump has been working to identify ways to bring down costs, including by temporarily lifting restrictions on “red dye” diesel used in farm equipment.

Trump did not mention raising during his call with Putin the still unexplained death of a plague lab researcher.

Instead, the US president focused solely on diesel supplies, which have concerned Republicans as higher energy prices drive up other costs.

“Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Trump wrote.

Energy analysts quickly cast doubt on that assertion.

“So assuming this happens and Putin delivers — which would mean reversing the ban on diesel exports that has been in place for several months now — it would be a bandaid, nothing more,” Gregory Brew, an analyst with Eurasia Group’s Energy, Climate & Resources team, said in an email.

“I also have a strong suspicion Putin expects Ukraine to cease its attacks on refineries in exchange for doing Trump the favor. I have a hard time seeing Zelensky cooperate on that front,” Brew said.

This story has been updated with additional details.

CNN’s Victoria Butenko, Kosta Gak and Billy Stockwell contributed reporting.

CNN’s Victoria Butenko, Kosta Gak and Billy Stockwell contributed reporting.
